title: The Lark and Her Young Ones
text:
A lark built her nest in a field of young wheat in early spring. By summer her chicks were nearly ready to fly, and the wheat around them had ripened.

One day the farmer came with his son to look at the crop. It was time to harvest, he said; he would ask his neighbors to come and help reap it. The young larks heard this and told their mother in alarm. Where should they go? She told them there was no need to move yet. A man who leaves the work to his neighbors is not really in earnest.

A few days later the farmer returned. The grain was overripe and beginning to fall. This time he said he would send for his relatives and friends to help. Again the chicks were frightened, and again their mother calmed them. Relatives and friends have their own fields to see to.

Then the farmer came a third time and saw the crop spoiling. Tomorrow, he said, he and his son would come themselves at dawn, with whatever workers they could hire, and cut the wheat. When the lark heard that, she gathered her young and moved them out that very night. Now, she said, the man meant it.
lesson: To judge whether something will really happen, ask who is actually going to do it. Plans that depend on others are often just talk; plans someone owns get done.
people: A lark, her chicks, a farmer and his son
caveat: Versions differ in the number of visits and who the farmer first relies on.
